subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Type Ia Supernovae: Standard Candles
description: A 60-second lesson on Type Ia Supernovae: Standard Candles.

hook.text: A white dwarf steals gas from a companion star until it hits a critical mass—and detonates completely.

buildup.text: Because the explosion always happens at the same mass, every Type Ia supernova has nearly the same brightness.

discovery.text: Astronomers use them as 'standard candles'—if you know the true brightness, you can calculate the distance.

twist.text: In 1998, Type Ia supernovae revealed that the universe's expansion is accelerating—driven by dark energy.

climax.text: Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess won the 2011 Nobel Prize for this discovery.

punchline.text: Exploding white dwarfs revealed dark energy. Dead stars lit the way.

quiz.question: How did Type Ia supernovae help discover dark energy?
options: Their consistent brightness allowed measuring distances that showed the universe is accelerating
They emitted dark energy particles detected by ground-based labs
Their explosions slowed down over time, revealing a hidden force

details.summary: Type Ia supernovae occur when a white dwarf in a binary system accretes enough matter to exceed the Chandrasekhar limit (1.4 solar masses), triggering thermonuclear detonation.
details.whyItMatters: Type Ia supernovae are the 'standard candles' that revealed the universe's accelerating expansion — the discovery of dark energy. Their consistent brightness allows astronomers to measure distances across billions of light-years.
takeaways: They occur when white dwarfs exceed 1.4 solar masses
Consistent peak brightness makes them standard candles
They revealed the universe's accelerating expansion

faq.question: How did Type Ia supernovae lead to discovering dark energy?
faq.answer: In 1998, two teams measured distances to distant Type Ia supernovae and found they were farther away than expected — the universe's expansion is accelerating, not slowing. This implied a mysterious repulsive force, dubbed dark energy, earning the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

faq.question: Are all Type Ia supernovae exactly the same brightness?
faq.answer: Not exactly, but their variations are well-understood. Brighter ones fade more slowly (the Phillips relationship), allowing correction for differences. After correction, they're consistent enough to measure distances with about 5% precision — remarkable across billions of light-years.
